title: Information Architecture For Expert Systems
excerpt: Information architecture for expert systems defines how complex information spaces are structured, labelled, navigated and progressively disclosed. The capability applies when expert tools must match domain mental models, preserve governance traceability, and support deep workflows in a single working environment.
metaDescription: How information architecture structures object models, navigation, disclosure and traceability in complex expert systems.

definition: Information architecture for expert systems is the structural organisation of an expert information space: how entities are defined, grouped, labelled, navigated, disclosed and related so that the system matches the domain mental model and supports the user's actual work.

bodyMarkdown:
## Summary

Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

Information architecture for expert systems is the structural organisation of a complex information space. It defines how entities are named, grouped, related, navigated and progressively disclosed so that the system matches the way domain experts organise their work.

In Creative Navy's documentation, information architecture is not limited to menu design. It includes object models, navigation models, process structures, governance structures, evidence continuity, disclosure depth, support identifiers, and rules for what earns a place in the interface at all.

## When information architecture for expert systems is needed

Information architecture becomes a primary design problem when the system's existing structure reflects implementation history, internal database logic, organisational ownership, or accumulated product decisions rather than the user's domain logic.

In the Gexcon CFD simulation case, 15 years of feature addition had produced a navigation structure that reflected the history of the software's development rather than the logic of the engineering work it supported. The redesign had to support 102 documented tasks in a single working environment.

In the Polymatica OLAP analytics case, the information architecture was built around OLAP concepts such as the cube metaphor, dimensions, facts and SQL-level connection flows. Those structures were legible to database specialists but opaque to the data analysts who needed to use the product.

In the Puraite case, the original navigation had 13 top-level items organised around the product's internal structure. Creative Navy identified the navigation issue outside the original scope and restructured it into 4 top-level items that followed the four stages of systematic review.

## What information architecture for expert systems does

Creative Navy's information architecture work defines the structural model that makes an expert system navigable, explainable and usable without removing the domain complexity that the system must preserve.

The capability includes object modelling: identifying the entities that carry the work, such as projects, datasets, policies, cohorts, tasks, parts, orders, vessels, workflows or operating contexts. In the Callsign fraud detection case, separating the AI scoring model from the policy layer was an information-architecture decision as well as a technical decision. Policy became the central object, bundling conditions, actions, history and links to related rules.

The capability includes navigation modelling: defining the explicit rules governing how users move through the system and access content. In the industrial engagement for a European industrial automation vendor, customers configured the interface themselves; an administrator selected which components a group needed, and that selection generated the group's navigation. The audit finding in that system was specific: navigation changed between screens, seven rail icons appeared on operator screens and thirteen elsewhere, machine strip membership and order shifted, one machine was absent from one view, and no navigation item carried a text label.

The capability includes mental-model alignment: replacing structures that make sense to the producer of information with structures that make sense to the person consuming it. In Assemblio, the parts list was flattened so that each part carried a quantity. The structure was refined into two tabs: parts needed for the current step, and the full hierarchy. The principle is that the structure correct for the person who created the data is frequently wrong for the person who consumes it, and the fix can be a different view rather than a different database.

## Object models, navigation models and process structures

Information architecture for expert systems often starts with the question of which object should organise the system.

In Polymatica, the central object became the dataset rather than the OLAP cube. The Dataset Manager acted as a central orientation point: a card-based view of datasets showing dimensions, measures, record count, last updated date and notes. Users opened the application to datasets, and datasets became the entry point to operations. This solved a comprehension problem, not only a navigation problem.

In Callsign, policy became the central object. Fraud rules had been scattered across database views and configuration tables, reflecting how the system was built internally rather than how fraud analysts reason about fraud strategy. The model/policy separation clarified the system's conceptual structure and made the policy interface designable.

In Egma Order, four genuinely different transaction shapes had to sit under one navigation and one form grammar: RX, Stock, Bulk Stock and Services, alongside Home, the Order Center, Get Help and Master. The before-and-after decision tree shows the shift from many simultaneously available decision points after login to four top-level branches: order lenses, order services, track an order and get support.

In Puraite, the navigation was structured around the user's process rather than the product's internal architecture. The four-item navigation matched the four stages of systematic review. This is process-structured navigation: the organising principle is the work sequence, not the software implementation.

## Progressive disclosure and progressive specification

Creative Navy uses progressive disclosure in expert systems when users need a clear entry point but the full depth of the system must remain accessible.

In the Hudex intelligence analysis platform, the dondogram, a hierarchical AI clustering visualisation, had been the primary entry point. The information architecture added a project overview layer before the dondogram: a project cover page with high-level theme counts, source counts and orientation information. The project overview went through 20 iterations, the highest iteration count for any single component in the portfolio.

In the Raymarine fixed-mount VHF case, information architecture had to work on a 480 × 272 instrument. The design used four primary screens — radio, AIS target list, AIS compact plot and own vessel — traversed by a directional keypad when no overlay owned focus, with contextual, transaction, safety and system screens layered beneath. The engagement refused a global mode split between basic and advanced interfaces; one consistent model with shortcuts and progressive disclosure was selected instead.

Progressive specification is different from progressive disclosure. It means the information architecture supports iterative refinement rather than one-time navigation to content. In Akrivia, cohort construction had to support iterative hypothesis development and institutional auditability. Five interaction models were developed and evaluated: wizard, nested logic blocks, timeline, fragment reuse and side-by-side comparison. Each model represented a different structural hypothesis about how researchers think about cohort construction.

## Information architecture as governance structure

Information architecture becomes governance architecture when the system must preserve provenance, decision history or reviewability.

In Akrivia, the structural tension was between researcher analytical freedom and institutional auditability. The design position identified in Concept Convergence was the point where those requirements aligned: the query structure was automatically visible and reproducible through the architecture, rather than requiring researchers to document it separately. Client-reported evidence states that governance reviewers could verify cohort logic without escalating to the research team.

In Callsign, the policy engine's governance structure was what risk teams at Lloyds and HSBC could evaluate under SCA and PCI DSS requirements. The information architecture made policy an inspectable object with conditions, actions, history and links to related rules.

In the MDU ship motion monitor, the log was split into an alarm log, an event log of settings changes with before-and-after values, and a timeline. Alarm and settings records were kept indefinitely because their value was as an index into the raw sensor record rather than as a record in themselves.

In the maritime traffic software portfolio, the transferable structure was the context ticket: a typed reference carrying sector, selected track, source, time mode and originating surface. The context ticket was propagated through transitions and used for return navigation and keyboard focus restoration. The audit's primary finding was not a missing function; required functions existed in separate panels and views. What was not preserved was the evidence about a vessel, its source, the operator's action and the ongoing task.

## Information architecture in constrained devices and physical contexts

Information architecture for expert systems is not restricted to software running on general-purpose screens. The same structural questions apply when physical use conditions or display constraints determine navigation.

In the MDU ship motion monitor, navigation was decided by a physical unknown rather than by content. The unit's position relative to its reader could not be predicted, so bottom navigation was chosen over both sidebars and a hamburger menu. A sidebar correct for someone standing to the left would force someone standing to the right to reach across and cover the display; the scarce resource in the layout was horizontal space, not vertical.

In AIT's heat pump controller work, the source structure was roughly 900 nodes across eleven hierarchy levels, in German, and changed during the design block. The settings space the new interface had to absorb included roughly 135 commissioning parameters and 98 numbered fault codes, with parameters hidden by access level and detected heat pump variant. The settings structure was kept close to the one installers already knew, with a breadcrumb trail and a unique numeric identifier on every menu item. The numbered-identifier convention served telephone support rather than navigation.

In Streetec kntrl 2, settings were kept as a single scrolling list rather than nested categories. Category labels would have presupposed the technical vocabulary that a non-expert user did not have. The client's own experience of a competitor's product reinforced that failure pattern: users could know a function existed while not knowing which menu contained it.

## Standards-grounded information architecture

Topera is the distinct case in this capability because its information architecture was built from formal sources rather than from analysis of an existing deployed system. Creative Navy produced a concept design for Topera; nothing has been built, and there is no product, deployment or user.

The Topera architecture was designed as a matrix with two axes. The horizontal time axis carried the five DIN 69901-2 lifecycle phases. The vertical knowledge axis carried eleven management domains. Every cell was populated with the DIN 69901-2 processes active in that phase, the DIN 69901-4 data model entities that carry the information, and the PSI 25 synchronisation activity that propagates it to partners.

Every Topera screen specification carried its standard reference and synchronisation level. The architecture was required to be complete even where the MVP was not; non-implemented areas had to appear as future extension points. Both navigation axes were designed as real routes rather than one primary and one secondary route. All fourteen DIN 69901-2 Mindeststandard processes appeared by their standard process codes in the mapping and design requirements documents. This is a coverage check, not a conformance claim.

## Shared context and persistent operating shells

Information architecture for expert systems often has to decide what state is shared across workspaces and what state belongs only to a local task.

In KISPE Space, the design used six logical workspaces: Operating Picture, Imagery, Satellite Services, Environment, Briefings and System Status as a global utility. A hybrid architecture was adopted over two alternatives that were built and assessed. The hybrid kept a small, explicit shared context — confirmed area, temporal perspective and return path — while giving each task workspace its own layout. The accepted cost was named: shared state is more complex, local filters must never be misrepresented as global, and a persistent header costs real pixels on a compact device.

In Schone Airspace Group Mission Control, the application was organised around the operator's task rather than the underlying subsystem. Planning and Review were top-level destinations. Flight, Camera and Fleet were peer views inside a persistent live operating environment. Readiness acted as a controlled transition between a prepared mission and a live session. The accepted cost was that the navigation structure was larger than a single dashboard, in exchange for each screen having a more predictable responsibility.

In the maritime traffic software portfolio, a summary dashboard landing view was built and rejected. It was attractive for commercial presentations, but it moved the active traffic picture into a secondary container and forced operators to reacquire sector, object and layer context after every inspection. The dockable inspector was chosen because it preserved the active traffic picture while allowing contextual investigation.

## Deciding what earns a place in the interface

Some information-architecture work concerns inclusion rather than organisation. The handheld C2 engagement is the clearest example in this capability.

The client was a European manufacturer of uncrewed systems, including one-way effectors, and the tactical command-and-control software that operates them. Creative Navy's work covered interface structure, task behaviour, information priority and the clarity of operator control. It did not extend to autonomy, control algorithms, the datalink, the effector, targeting logic, or any certification or weapons-review activity.

The transferable artefact was a decision model for inclusion. Every element and control was tested against a named operator question, assigned to a function that owned it, and classified as persistent, contextual or alert-driven. Information that could not answer one of the questions was a candidate for removal, consolidation or secondary placement.

The five-function decomposition behind the model was Aviate, Navigate and Execute the Mission as the primary trio, with Command and Control and Manage Contingencies as cross-cutting functions. The structure was adapted from published NASA, FAA and EASA uncrewed-aircraft human-factors guidance rather than copied from any one framework.

## What information architecture for expert systems produces

Creative Navy's information architecture work can produce task inventories, object models, navigation models, disclosure structures, process maps, decision trees, inclusion models, context-continuity mechanisms and standards-traceable architecture maps.

In Gexcon, 102 tasks were documented with goals, frequency, difficulty, actions and hierarchy of needs within sequences. The task documentation was the prerequisite for the information architecture redesign.

In Polymatica, 45 structural variants were explored across 10 challenge areas before convergence. The result replaced the technical OLAP-centred model with a dataset-centred model and distinguished guided linear tasks from open exploration tasks.

In Egma Order, roughly 7,000 lens types were made navigable by three moves in sequence: repeat a past order first; filter by eight criteria; then use a quantities step in which the interface auto-calculates the percentage each lens type represents of the total.

In Schone Airspace Group Mission Control, ten information priority matrices specified 97 individual information placements on a four-level scale: operationally critical, task essential, supporting and reference. The placements were organised by workspace and operating condition rather than by software subsystem.

## Evidence basis for information architecture outcomes

The evidence for information architecture outcomes differs by case and should not be treated as a single evidence category.

In Gexcon, active users per team increased from 1 to 3–4 according to client-reported evidence. The case records the information architecture change as the mechanism: when non-specialist roles such as risk managers and safety analysts could navigate the system without requiring specialist guidance, the user base expanded. The case evidence also records time to first successful simulation changing from 4 days to 6 hours; the notes identify this as measured, but do not specify the canonical measurement subtype.

In Polymatica, independent task completion increased from 2% to 56% in product analytics. The information architecture change is recorded as a primary mechanism: users who could not form a mental model of the system could not complete basic operations, and completion rates increased when the structure matched their mental model.

In Akrivia, the evidence is client-reported: governance reviewers could verify cohort logic without escalating to the research team. In Puraite, the client described the navigation restructuring as one of the most significant contributions of the engagement. In Hudex, the available evidence records 20 iterations on the project overview component.

Some entries are design-reasoning evidence rather than outcome evidence. AIT and the MDU are explicitly design reasoning only, with no user testing reported. Topera is a concept design only and has no outcome of any kind.

## Boundaries and limits

Information architecture for expert systems does not mean simplifying every structure. In Gexcon, the central question was the difference between essential complexity and accidental complexity. Essential complexity was load-bearing scientific rigour; accidental complexity was historical sediment from 15 years of development.

Information architecture for expert systems also does not always replace lists with richer structures. In Assemblio's synchronisation work, part-level matching presented a list of hundreds of part substitutions that could not be collapsed because each row carried a human approval for liability reasons. Creative Navy's conclusion to the client was that a search field helps, and if the planner must decide part by part, there may be no better representation than a list.

The documented cases do not establish universal patterns for all expert systems. Hub-and-spoke information architecture, flat information architecture and hierarchical information architecture have different implications depending on the domain logic. The correct structure is determined by the work being supported, the object model, the user mental model, the governance requirement and the constraints of the operating environment.

## Related pages

Information architecture for expert systems is closely related to workflow and task structure redesign because both capabilities organise work around the user's actual process. It also connects to cognitive load reduction when structure reduces unnecessary search, orientation and vocabulary burden.

The capability overlaps with behavioural governance for AI products where information architecture makes policy, provenance or review logic inspectable. It overlaps with state and status visibility design where navigation must preserve shared context, selection, focus or evidence across transitions.
